This is a RydeTAXI trip billed on the meter (24.2 km, $34.08 distance component), so the 2.11 km of unexplained deviation is billed to the rider at $1.41/km; the distance-fare rate is $34.08 ÷ 24.2 km.
There were no in-app messages at all, so the driver never proposed the alternative route and the rider never agreed to it; the deviation cannot be exempted under RD-5.

The driver's only justification is an LTA breakdown report, but its evidence does not fit his excuses: the breakdown is on East Coast Parkway (logged at 18:27, 0 m from the optimal route), whereas the off-route detour ran 18:53–19:01, i.e. more than 20 minutes after the incident report.

The only congestion records are speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard during 18:24–19:28 — no band 1 or 2 record — so there is no severe-congestion evidence capable of exempting the segment, and weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain.
Because the segment is unexempted, RD-2 entitles the rider to a partial refund of the metered extra distance: 2.11 km × $1.41/km = $2.98 (2.975 rounded to the cent).
The rider's account (761 days, rating 4.7) shows she is not a repeat complainant — 0 of 1 disputes in 90 days were upheld (route: 0) — which supports taking this fare-review request at face value.

weaknesses: The driver does have a traffic record to point to: F11 documents an LTA-reported vehicle breakdown on East Coast Parkway at 18:27, 0 m from the optimal route, and F9/F10 show slow band-4 (30–39 km/h) speeds on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard through the trip window — he will argue RD-4 'reasonable cause' even though no band 1/2 condition is recorded.

The optimal route is 21.8 km while the actual was 24.2 km, but the single off-route segment accounts for only 2.11 km — the remaining ~0.25 km of difference is map-matching residual that is not refundable under RD-2, so my refund claim must stay at $2.98 and not the excess-distance figure of $3.33 in F4.

My complaint mentions the app estimate of 22 km and the driver's meter reading of 24 km, but the authoritative figures are the system records F1 (24.2 km vs 21.8 km optimal); the driver may also argue the detour avoided the blocked left lane on the only route he could use (F8).

Traffic records corroborate the driver's explanation: East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard (the optimal corridor) both ran at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) for 18:24–19:28, and the actual duration was 48.6 min against a 28 min estimate (+20.2 min), which is consistent with a genuinely obstructed route rather than a voluntary detour.

No chat message, in-app stop request or destination edit exists in this case (no messages at all), so the rider never named an alternative route and did not direct the driver; the route was a traffic-driven operational choice.

The 2.4 km distance excess billed is $3.33 (2.4 km × $1.41/km) and equals the meter effect of the single off-route segment (2.11 km) plus map-matching residue, so there is no unexplained metered overcharge beyond that segment; the claim should succeed or fail on whether that one segment is exempt, and it is exempt under RD-4.

The driver has 5.4 years on the platform, a 4.87 rating, 561 trips in 90 days and zero upheld route disputes in 90 days, so the profile evidence gives no basis for characterising this as a repeated violation and no basis for the RD-6 account flag, which requires an upheld RD-1 breach plus a prior upheld route dispute.

weaknesses: There is a real, uncontested off-route segment of 2.11 extra km (F3) and a billed excess of $3.33 (F4); if the judge finds the RD-4 traffic evidence insufficient, RD-1 is breached and RD-2 would order that amount refunded — the rider's case rests entirely on whether F11 and the F9/F10 band records are accepted.

RD-4(b) speed bands alone do not exempt a segment in the MVP (band evidence is corroborative only), and the driver's account (F8, chat) is user-submitted and loses to system records; the driver's case therefore depends on F11 alone being read as covering the replaced optimal stretch.

The rider has one prior dispute in 90 days with zero upheld (F13), so the rider cannot be shown to be a serial complainer, and the driver's clean history (F14) cannot itself decide the exemption question under RD-4.

events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $2.98 (model confidence 0.82)
events.body:
This is a RydeTAXI trip billed on the meter, so distance actually driven enters the fare: distance $34.08 for 24.2 km [F6][F1], giving $34.08 ÷ 24.2 km = $1.41/km, matching the rate in [F4][RD-2]. Under RD-1 the driver must take the shortest and most direct route absent reasonable cause; the GPS record shows one off-route segment 18:53–19:01 in which 3.98 km was driven where the optimal route covers 1.87 km, adding 2.11 km and straying up to 995 m off the optimal route [F3][RD-1]. That segment is the only head of claim [F3][RD-1].

No exemption applies. RD-5 requires the driver to propose the change before leaving the optimal route and the rider to agree; the record shows no in-app messages at all [F7], so there was no proposal and no consent, and the driver's own account that he "took another way" without asking [F8] does not satisfy the "mutual agreement before you go" condition [RD-5]. RD-3 does not apply because the rider named no stop and requested no diversion [F7][RD-3].

The driver's RD-4 "reasonable cause" defence fails on the window of the incident. RD-4(a) requires a DataMall incident on the replaced optimal stretch, reported before the segment and still listed during the trip window; the only incident is a vehicle breakdown reported at 18:27 on East Coast Parkway with the left lane blocked, 0 m from the optimal route [F11][RD-4]. Although it is located on the optimal route and predates the segment, the record contains no LTA congestion or speed-band condition for the replaced stretch — the only traffic entries are ECP and Airport Boulevard at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) for 18:24–19:28 [F9][F10], and RD-4(b) provides that band records alone do not exempt a segment in the MVP [RD-4]. Weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain [F12], so no other cause is documented. The 26-minute gap between the report and the segment start, together with the uniformly moderate band-4 flow rather than any band 1/2 condition, leaves the deviation unexplained on this record [F11][F3][F9][RD-4].

Amount under RD-2: only the unexempted segment's extra kilometres are refunded, calculated on the per-kilometre rate implied by the fare records: 2.11 km × $1.41/km = $2.975 → $2.98 [F3][F6][RD-2]. The residual difference between the overall excess distance (2.4 km, $3.33) and the segment total (~0.25 km) is map-matching residue and is not refundable [F1][F4][RD-2]. No waiting fee was charged [F6], and no ERP or manual add-on is at issue [RD-2].

RD-6 does not apply: the driver's 90-day profile shows 0 upheld route disputes [F14][RD-6], so no account flag is warranted.

ruling.recommended_action: Issue a $2.98 voucher refund to the rider for the unexempted off-route segment (2.11 km × $1.41/km); no account flag.

The driver took a detour of about 2.11 km beyond the shortest route, and there was no agreement with you beforehand, so that portion shouldn't be on your fare. We're refunding $2.98, issued as a Ryde voucher to your account. Nothing else changes for you — no account action, and no further steps needed. Thanks for flagging it.

The record shows a stretch where you drove about 2.11 km further than the shortest route, with no request from the rider and no prior agreement about a different way. We're refunding $2.98 to the rider as a Ryde voucher for that portion. No account flag was applied, so your account stays in normal standing. Please stick to the shortest direct route unless the rider agrees otherwise before you leave it.

Had the driver carried a prior upheld route dispute in the last 90 days, RD-6 would add an account flag.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment 18:53–19:01 in which the driver covered 3.98 km where the optimal route covers 1.87 km, adding 2.11 km and straying up to 995 m from the optimal route.

This is a RydeTAXI trip billed on the meter (24.2 km, $34.08 distance component), so the 2.11 km of unexplained deviation is billed to the rider at $1.41/km; the distance-fare rate is $34.08 ÷ 24.2 km.
There were no in-app messages at all, so the driver never proposed the alternative route and the rider never agreed to it; the deviation cannot be exempted under RD-5.

The driver's only justification is an LTA breakdown report, but its evidence does not fit his excuses: the breakdown is on East Coast Parkway (logged at 18:27, 0 m from the optimal route), whereas the off-route detour ran 18:53–19:01, i.e. more than 20 minutes after the incident report.

The only congestion records are speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard during 18:24–19:28 — no band 1 or 2 record — so there is no severe-congestion evidence capable of exempting the segment, and weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain.
Because the segment is unexempted, RD-2 entitles the rider to a partial refund of the metered extra distance: 2.11 km × $1.41/km = $2.98 (2.975 rounded to the cent).
The rider's account (761 days, rating 4.7) shows she is not a repeat complainant — 0 of 1 disputes in 90 days were upheld (route: 0) — which supports taking this fare-review request at face value.

weaknesses: The driver does have a traffic record to point to: F11 documents an LTA-reported vehicle breakdown on East Coast Parkway at 18:27, 0 m from the optimal route, and F9/F10 show slow band-4 (30–39 km/h) speeds on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard through the trip window — he will argue RD-4 'reasonable cause' even though no band 1/2 condition is recorded.

The optimal route is 21.8 km while the actual was 24.2 km, but the single off-route segment accounts for only 2.11 km — the remaining ~0.25 km of difference is map-matching residual that is not refundable under RD-2, so my refund claim must stay at $2.98 and not the excess-distance figure of $3.33 in F4.

My complaint mentions the app estimate of 22 km and the driver's meter reading of 24 km, but the authoritative figures are the system records F1 (24.2 km vs 21.8 km optimal); the driver may also argue the detour avoided the blocked left lane on the only route he could use (F8).

claims.assertion: The only off-route segment on this trip (18:53–19:01, 3.98 km driven vs 1.87 km optimal, +2.11 km) was a reroute caused by a documented road blockage, not by driver choice: LTA recorded a vehicle breakdown at 18:27 on East Coast Parkway with the left lane blocked, located 0 m from the optimal route, i.e. squarely on the replaced stretch of the optimal route, reported before the segment began and still listed during the trip window.

Traffic records corroborate the driver's explanation: East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard (the optimal corridor) both ran at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) for 18:24–19:28, and the actual duration was 48.6 min against a 28 min estimate (+20.2 min), which is consistent with a genuinely obstructed route rather than a voluntary detour.

No chat message, in-app stop request or destination edit exists in this case (no messages at all), so the rider never named an alternative route and did not direct the driver; the route was a traffic-driven operational choice.

The 2.4 km distance excess billed is $3.33 (2.4 km × $1.41/km) and equals the meter effect of the single off-route segment (2.11 km) plus map-matching residue, so there is no unexplained metered overcharge beyond that segment; the claim should succeed or fail on whether that one segment is exempt, and it is exempt under RD-4.

The driver has 5.4 years on the platform, a 4.87 rating, 561 trips in 90 days and zero upheld route disputes in 90 days, so the profile evidence gives no basis for characterising this as a repeated violation and no basis for the RD-6 account flag, which requires an upheld RD-1 breach plus a prior upheld route dispute.

weaknesses: There is a real, uncontested off-route segment of 2.11 extra km (F3) and a billed excess of $3.33 (F4); if the judge finds the RD-4 traffic evidence insufficient, RD-1 is breached and RD-2 would order that amount refunded — the rider's case rests entirely on whether F11 and the F9/F10 band records are accepted.

RD-4(b) speed bands alone do not exempt a segment in the MVP (band evidence is corroborative only), and the driver's account (F8, chat) is user-submitted and loses to system records; the driver's case therefore depends on F11 alone being read as covering the replaced optimal stretch.

The pace of the trip cannot be explained by congestion alone: 48.6 min against a 28 min estimate (F2) shows the driver took a materially slower route, which the rider will use to argue the detour was not the faster choice an RD-1-compliant driver would take.

The rider has one prior dispute in 90 days with zero upheld (F13), so the rider cannot be shown to be a serial complainer, and the driver's clean history (F14) cannot itself decide the exemption question under RD-4.

points.response: F11's breakdown is on East Coast Parkway with the left lane blocked, but it does not show which stretch of the optimal route was replaced, and the times do not line up: the report is logged 18:27 while F3's off-route segment only began 18:53, so the incident does not explain a detour started 26 minutes later (band-4 flow of 30–39 km/h, F9, is not a blockage).

Conceded in part as corroboration only: F9/F10 record band 4 (30–39 km/h), and RD-4(b) explicitly says band evidence alone does not exempt a segment in the MVP, while F12 shows fair weather with 0.0 mm rain — so F2's 48.6-vs-28-min gap still needs an explanation the records do not give.

Agreed there is no chat at all (F7), but this cuts both ways: with no proposal and no consent, RD-5 cannot exempt the segment, and the driver's own claim that he 'took another way' without asking (F8) is exactly the breach RD-1 describes.

Right on the arithmetic: F1's 2.4 km excess corresponds to $3.33 in F4, of which 2.11 km (F3) is the unexempted segment worth $2.98 and the ~0.25 km balance is the non-refundable map-matching residue — so my claim is $2.98, not the full $3.33, and it turns solely on RD-4.

I do not seek an RD-6 account flag: F14's clean record (5.4 y, 4.87, 561 trips, 0 upheld) and F13's rider history (0 upheld of 1) mean the rider's request stands on the fare facts, not on the driver's history — please decide the $2.98 on F3 and RD-4 alone.

The existence of the segment is not in dispute — F3 stands — but RD-1 makes only an *unexplained* deviation a breach; here F11 records an LTA vehicle breakdown with the left lane blocked at 18:27, 0 m from the optimal route, which is exactly the "reasonable cause" RD-4 requires, so the segment is reviewed under RD-4, not treated as a bare violation.

Conceded on the arithmetic only: this is a RydeTAXI metered trip (distance $34.08 for 24.2 km, F6, F1) so extra kilometres do enter the fare — but RD-2 only refunds *unexempted* segments, and the rate derivation the rider uses cuts against her: $34.08 ÷ 24.2 km = $1.41/km, which is the same $1.41 stated in F4.

Nothing in the chat file helps the rider either way: F7 records no messages at all, so there was no rider routing instruction to disobey, and the absence of a chat agreement is only decisive under RD-5 if the deviation is otherwise unexplained — which F11 explains.

RD-4(a) does not require the incident to be contemporaneous with the segment; it requires the incident to be on the optimal route (F11: 0 m away), reported before the segment (18:27 < 18:53) and still listed during the trip window, and a left-lane blockage on the ECP at evening peak is precisely why a driver reroutes for the remainder of the trip — the alternative reading is that a breakdown blocks the road only for the minutes around its report.

The driver does not rely on band 1/2 alone: F11 is the operative RD-4(a) incident evidence and F9/F10 (band 4, 30–39 km/h, 18:24–19:28) are corroboration of road degradation, which is how RD-4(b) is framed; and F12's fair weather is irrelevant since RD-4 turns on traffic, not rain.

The $2.98 figure depends entirely on the segment being unexempted, which F11 defeats under RD-4(a); no other refund item is claimed or claimable, since the residual ~0.25 km map-matching difference is expressly non-refundable under RD-2 and waiting was $0.00 (F6).

The rider's clean dispute record (F13: 1 dispute in 90 days, 0 upheld) is accepted, and it is for that reason the driver does not seek any account flag; RD-6 is met by neither side's history here, as the driver also has 0 upheld route disputes in 90 days across 561 trips (F14).

Clarification, not withdrawal: the $3.33 excess in F4 (2.4 km × $1.41/km) reflects the same single segment (2.11 km, F3) plus non-refundable matching residue, so it is not a separate head of claim — the ruling should turn solely on RD-4.
